title: Check the tools installed in Kali
command:
command -v burpsuite gobuster dirbuster subfinder ffuf curl jq
gobuster dir --help
ffuf -h
explanation: A handbook example does not mean its tool is installed. Inspect available programs before choosing an exercise.
options: command -v reports executable paths. Individual help commands describe your installed release. Use the Kali tool catalog for package names; do not assume every product has an apt package.
result: Paths for installed tools and help or a missing-command diagnostic.

title: Build the local practice website
command:
mkdir -p "$HOME/kali-lab/web-practice/site/help" printf 'Web practiceHelp ' > "$HOME/kali-lab/web-practice/site/index.html" printf '

Public help

' > "$HOME/kali-lab/web-practice/site/help/index.html" printf 'User-agent: * Disallow: /training-only/ ' > "$HOME/kali-lab/web-practice/site/robots.txt" printf 'help robots.txt missing-page ' > "$HOME/kali-lab/web-practice/words.txt"
explanation: Create a tiny static site and three candidate paths. Run this inside Kali. These commands replace only the named practice files.
options: The help directory exists, robots.txt exists, and missing-page does not. The robots rule is a hint, not access control; training-only is deliberately absent.
result: A repeatable directory-discovery exercise.

title: Serve the practice website
explanation: Run after building the site. Keep this terminal open and use another terminal for requests.
options: Loopback binding keeps the service inside Kali. Ctrl+C stops it. This static server has no login, database, TLS or vulnerable API.
result: HTTP service on http://127.0.0.1:8877/.

title: Read the HTTP conversation
explanation: An HTTP exchange contains a request method and path, headers, and sometimes a body; the response adds a status code.
options: -i includes response headers; --max-time limits total request time. Identify status, Content-Type, Content-Length and the HTML body.
result: 200 and the training page, if the server is running.

title: Compare existing and missing paths
explanation: A baseline makes discovery results interpretable. Compare a known resource with a deliberately absent one.
options: Expect 200 versus 404 in this lab. Real applications may return a login page or a 200 error page for both. Status alone cannot establish exposure.
result: Two responses with different status and body.

title: Inspect redirects before following them
explanation: A directory without its trailing slash normally redirects to the slash path in this server.
options: -I sends HEAD. Inspect Location; on real applications verify its destination is in scope before following. HEAD can behave differently from GET.
result: Normally 301 with Location: /help/.

title: Save reproducible response evidence
explanation: Keep response headers separate from the body so later comparisons have clear inputs.
options: -D writes headers and -o writes body; named files are replaced. Record time, URL, identity and tool version separately. A hash tracks file changes, not application safety.
result: Two evidence files and a body digest.

title: Inspect browser requests
command:
Open the local site in your browser.
Open Developer Tools > Network.
Reload; select the document request.
Inspect headers, response and timing.
explanation: The browser network panel connects user actions to HTTP requests.
options: Use a separate lab profile. A HAR export can contain cookies, tokens and personal data; remove sensitive fields from any shared copy.
result: A request inventory you can compare with curl.

title: Build an authorization test matrix
command:
Role | Action | Own object | Other test user object | Expected decision
Guest | View private profile | N/A | Deny | Login required
User A | View profile | Allow | Deny | Object ownership enforced
Admin | Support lookup | Policy | Policy | Audited access
explanation: Use two consenting test accounts and synthetic records in an application designed for the exercise.
options: Repeat the same read-only request as each identity. Change only the synthetic object identifier. Compare returned data, not merely HTTP status. The static practice server cannot run this test.
result: A documented allow/deny matrix and any minimal reproducible mismatch.

title: Write a finding and retest plan
command:
Title and affected route
Scope, time, application build and test role
Expected behavior and observed behavior
Minimal reproduction using synthetic data
Redacted request and response evidence
Impact, root cause and remediation
Retest steps, result and remaining limitations
explanation: A report turns an observation into an actionable engineering task.
options: Avoid treating a fingerprint or scanner alert as confirmed exploitation. Retest both the original failing case and a legitimate permitted case after remediation.
result: A finding another tester can reproduce without guessing.

title: Start Burp Suite
explanation: Launch the Kali-packaged Burp desktop application.
options: Use a temporary project for the first exercise. Save features differ by edition; do not assume every Community workflow persists between launches.
result: Burp startup or project screen.

title: Use the embedded browser
command:
Proxy > Open browser
Visit http://127.0.0.1:8877/
Keep interception off while browsing initially.
explanation: The embedded browser simplifies proxy setup for the first local exercise.
options: Use the practice service from the foundations chapter. Browser traffic can include unrelated requests; verify host and port before sending any request again.
result: The local page appears and its traffic is recorded.

title: Restrict the visible target
command:
Find http://127.0.0.1:8877 in Target / Site map.
Add this exact origin to scope.
Filter HTTP history to in-scope traffic.
explanation: Scope keeps investigation focused on the exercise.
options: Check scheme, address and port. A history filter changes visibility; it is not a network firewall and does not by itself constrain every extension or tool.
result: A focused history view.

title: Read Proxy history
command:
Proxy > HTTP history
Select GET / on port 8877.
Inspect the request and response panels.
explanation: History records what actually traveled through the proxy.
options: Locate Host, request path, status and HTML body. Use time and request sequence to correlate one browser action with several network exchanges.
result: An HTTP exchange you can explain field by field.

title: Intercept one harmless request
command:
Turn Intercept on.
Refresh the local page.
Inspect the paused GET, then Forward it.
Turn Intercept off.
explanation: Interception pauses traffic before delivery.
options: A browser that keeps loading may simply be waiting for Forward. Drop discards a request. Do not replay purchase, delete or other state-changing actions as practice.
result: The request completes after forwarding.

title: Compare paths in Repeater
command:
Send the local GET request to Repeater.
Send GET /.
Change only the path to /missing-page.
Send again and compare.
explanation: Repeater lets you change one variable and inspect the response.
options: Keep host and port fixed. Save notes describing the baseline and changed request, so a difference is attributable to your edit.
result: 200 for / and 404 for the missing path.

title: Understand encoding with Decoder
command:
Open Decoder.
Enter: hello%20lab
Decode as URL encoding.
Compare with the original text.
explanation: Encoding represents characters; it does not provide secrecy.
options: The decoded result is hello lab. Encode once for the intended protocol layer; repeated decoding may change meaning. Never paste real access tokens into online decoders.
result: A reversible text transformation.

title: Compare response evidence
command:
Send baseline and changed responses to Comparer.
Choose a word or byte comparison.
Review status, headers and body changes.
explanation: Differential testing helps isolate meaningful behavior.
options: Timestamps, request IDs and anti-CSRF values may vary normally. Annotate these differences before concluding that an access-control or injection issue exists.
result: A comparison with meaningful and incidental differences separated.

title: Run a three-value Intruder exercise
command:
Send the local GET / request to Intruder.
Clear automatic positions.
Mark only the path segment after /.
Use simple payloads: help/, robots.txt, missing-page.
Use one concurrent request and run once.
explanation: Use the three known paths to learn payload positions and response tables.
options: Keep the attack to one position and three values. Community throughput and controls differ from Professional. This is content comparison, not password guessing.
result: Three candidate-path results plus any tool housekeeping requests.

title: Plan authenticated testing
command:
Create two lab identities with different roles.
Record login and logout behavior.
Confirm which cookie or token identifies each account.
Repeat one harmless account-specific read as each user.
explanation: Authentication proves identity; authorization decides what that identity may access.
options: Use a deliberately configured training app. Keep cookie jars separate, verify the active user, and refresh expired sessions. A login redirect can masquerade as a negative security result.
result: Evidence linked to the correct account and role.

title: Use Scanner with explicit limits
command:
Professional edition: select a scoped training request.
Review the scan configuration and insertion points.
Choose the smallest relevant audit.
Review generated traffic and manually validate each alert.
explanation: Burp automated Scanner is a Professional feature. Community users can follow manual proxy and Repeater exercises.
options: Active auditing sends extra requests and can change application state. A clean result has limited coverage; an alert needs reproduction and context.
result: A bounded audit with reviewed evidence.

title: Evaluate extensions and session automation
command:
Record a task the built-in tools cannot handle.
Review an extension source, permissions and network behavior.
Try it in a disposable project with synthetic data.
For session rules, test on one request before wider use.
explanation: Extensions execute code; session handling can alter many requests automatically.
options: Check that tokens are inserted only for intended hosts. Avoid installing extensions merely because they are popular; keep a reproducible record of versions and settings.
result: A controlled extension or session-handling decision.

title: Gobuster: discover the three practice paths
explanation: Gobuster tries candidate paths from a wordlist. Start the practice server first.
options: dir selects paths; -u sets the URL; -w supplies words. One thread and a per-thread delay keep this exercise small.
result: help redirects, robots.txt exists, and the missing path is normally excluded.

title: Gobuster: try selected file extensions
explanation: Extension expansion adds requests for each candidate.
options: Estimate request count before using a larger list. Words that already contain an extension may produce unhelpful combinations. Review local help for version differences.
result: Mostly missing variants on this deliberately small site.

title: Gobuster: choose the correct mode
explanation: DNS discovery asks a resolver about candidate names; virtual-host discovery varies HTTP host routing.
options: These are different from directory discovery and from Subfinder passive sources. Wildcard DNS and default virtual hosts create false positives. Do not assume each answer identifies a distinct application.
result: Installed mode-specific options without scanning a domain.

title: DirBuster: launch the graphical tool
explanation: DirBuster provides a graphical interface for wordlist-based path discovery.
options: Kali provides the Java application. Use local help if launch fails. Its interface and controls differ from Gobuster despite the similar purpose.
result: DirBuster window.

title: DirBuster: configure a small path search
command:
Target: http://127.0.0.1:8877/
Wordlist: ~/kali-lab/web-practice/words.txt (browse to the full path)
Threads: 1
Disable recursive searching for this exercise.
Start; review results; stop when the small list finishes.
explanation: Use the same tiny lab to compare graphical and terminal discovery.
options: Review directory/file mode and extensions because they change request count. A 403 response does not prove sensitive data is retrievable. Save the result and settings together.
result: A small path inventory comparable with Gobuster.

title: Wappalyzer: read technology fingerprints
command:
Install the official Wappalyzer browser extension in a lab profile.
Visit an authorized application.
Open the extension panel and record detected technologies.
explanation: Wappalyzer infers technologies from observable page and response signals.
options: Results can be incomplete or mistaken. Review extension permissions. Avoid testing a private authenticated application through an external lookup service without understanding data sharing.
result: Technology hypotheses to validate.

title: Wappalyzer: validate a version claim
command:
Record the detected product and any reported version.
Find a second independent signal.
Ask the application owner to verify the deployed build.
Record confidence and observation time.
explanation: A framework label or old banner is not proof of a vulnerable installation.
options: A reverse proxy, cached asset or customized header can mislead identification. Missing detections do not prove absence. Online lookup and API capabilities differ from the extension and may involve a crawl.
result: An inventory entry with evidence and uncertainty.

title: Subfinder: inspect available sources
explanation: Subfinder collects names from passive sources such as public datasets and provider APIs.
options: -ls lists sources. Provider credentials and availability affect coverage. Passive enumeration still sends queries to third-party services.
result: Help and source names.

title: Subfinder: query an owned domain
explanation: Run only after choosing a domain you own or have permission to assess.
options: -d supplies the domain; -silent reduces output; -o writes the result. Stop if the input is empty or not your approved domain. Provider limits and missing keys may reduce results.
result: Candidate names; no guarantee that each currently resolves.

title: Review names before active probing
explanation: Keep passive discovery separate from an active test target list.
options: Confirm each candidate against scope and owner inventory. Shared services, stale names and third-party delegations need review. Do not pipe an unreviewed list straight into scanners.
result: A deduplicated candidate list; q exits less.

title: ffuf: discover paths with a marker
explanation: ffuf replaces FUZZ with each line of the wordlist.
options: -t controls concurrency; -rate caps requests per second; -mc all initially shows all status codes so the negative baseline remains visible.
result: Results including the known missing path.

title: ffuf: filter after measuring a baseline
explanation: Filtering removes expected negative responses from the result view.
options: -fc 404 fits this static lab. For a soft-404 application, inspect response size, words and content before choosing a filter. Overbroad filtering can hide real endpoints.
result: Existing or redirecting paths; 404 results hidden.

title: ffuf: preserve structured results
explanation: A structured report supports repeatable comparisons.
options: Save the wordlist, version, scope and filter settings alongside it. The same response length across two pages does not establish identical content.
result: A JSON report, replacing the named report if present.

title: ProjectDiscovery httpx: inspect one service
explanation: ProjectDiscovery httpx summarizes HTTP endpoints. It is different from the Python HTTPX library.
options: Confirm httpx -h identifies the intended product. -sc shows status, -title the page title, -cl length; -nfs keeps the input scheme.
result: A compact summary of the practice service.

title: Katana: crawl local links
explanation: Katana follows links rather than guessing every possible path.
options: -d limits depth; -c and -p limit concurrency; -rl limits rate; -cs limits crawl scope. Review extracted URLs before treating them as authorized targets.
result: The linked help route may be discovered; robots.txt is not linked.

title: ZAP: begin with manual exploration
command:
Start ZAP and choose a temporary session.
Use Manual Explore with http://127.0.0.1:8877/.
Browse the local page and help link.
Inspect history and passive alerts.
explanation: ZAP is another intercepting proxy and assessment platform.
options: Use a different listener port if Burp already occupies 8080. Passive analysis examines proxied messages; spidering and active scanning generate additional traffic.
result: Traffic history and any passive observations.

title: Nuclei: inspect before choosing templates
explanation: Nuclei runs template-defined checks; the selected template determines requests and effects.
options: Read a template before running it: target paths, methods, payloads, matchers and callbacks. For this static lab choose a reviewed local informational template if available, not an entire template collection.
result: Help and a checklist for selecting a bounded check.

title: sqlmap: understand detection scope
explanation: sqlmap automates SQL injection testing. Its advanced options include operations far beyond detecting a suspected issue.
options: Learn only in an intentionally vulnerable isolated application with synthetic data. Fix the parameter, request, account and request budget first. The static Python server has no SQL backend and cannot demonstrate SQL injection.
result: Basic and extended help; no target requests.

title: jq: inspect a saved ffuf report
explanation: Local parsing lets you review evidence without sending more requests.
options: Run the structured ffuf example first. Keep the original report; this projection intentionally omits other fields.
result: URL, HTTP status and length for each recorded result.
